title: Anthropic and Adaptyv Bio open $2 million protein design competition — applications close today
subtitle: Five open challenges at the frontier of protein engineering, 5,000 experimental validations funded, $1M in Claude credits, Modal compute and Twist DNA on top — running September 28 through October 31 with open results.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic and Adaptyv Bio launched a five-challenge protein design competition on September 16, 2026, with applications closing today, September 24. The two organizations are jointly funding $1 million in experimental validation to test more than 5,000 protein designs in Adaptyv's automated wet lab, and Anthropic is adding $1 million in Claude credits for participants. Modal is providing up to $250,000 in compute credits and Twist Bioscience is supplying the DNA. Selected teams are notified before September 28, and the competition runs through October 31 with results published openly.

The five challenges target problems where current protein-design pipelines still struggle. Species cross-reactivity asks for binders that work across humans and animal models. pH-sensitivity asks for binders that release their target in a low-pH environment like the endosome. Peptide-MHC specificity is the immune-recognition problem behind personalized cancer therapy. And two of the challenges attack difficult G-protein-coupled receptors, the largest family of drug targets. None of these are toy benchmarks — solving any of them well would move real drug programs forward.

The launch sits alongside Anthropic's September 17 research post reporting that Claude, run as a general-purpose research model, optimized 36 open-source biomolecular modeling packages in under four weeks and delivered roughly a 4x average speed-up across co-folding, structure generation, inverse folding, genomics, and protein language models. That turns this competition into a live experiment about who — commercial protein-design startups, academic labs, or small teams armed with Claude and the newly-optimized open-source stack — actually wins the hard problems when compute is free and 5,000 designs get real wet-lab validation.

Takeaway for learners — this is the shape AI-for-science competitions are taking now. A real experimental budget attached, open results, and a short enough runway that a small team can plausibly win. If you are a bioengineering student or an ML person curious about biology, the barrier to entry has dropped from needing a lab to needing a well-scoped model of what a binder should do. Watch the results published in November — the leaderboard will tell you which methods actually generalize outside curated academic benchmarks.
